extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary students, critics, and educated readers of poetics
extracted.subtask_description: Elizabethan-era poetics: normative criteria for what poetry is and should do — its kinds, functions, manners, and moral effects (Sidney's standards for producing and judging poesy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Poesy as imitation with the end to teach and delight
rubrics_metrics.description: “Poesy ... is an art of imitation; for so Aristotle termeth it in the word μίμησις; that is to say, a representing, counterfeiting, or figuring forth: to speak metaphorically, a speaking picture, with this end, to teach and delight.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The fundamental criterion: a poem should imitate (represent) and accomplish both instruction and pleasure. Evaluate a poem by how well its imitation produces understanding (teaching) and pleasurable apprehension (delighting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Three kinds of poesy — chief (divine), philosophical, and true poets
rubrics_metrics.description: Sidney enumerates three general kinds: (1) the chief, which imitates the inconceivable excellencies of God (e.g., the Psalms); (2) those dealing with philosophical matter (moral, natural, astronomical, historical); (3) the third, true poets who freely invent what may be and should be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify which kind a work belongs to and judge by appropriate aims: divine/psalmic poesy for worship and prophecy; philosophical for conveying learned matter attractively; true poets for imaginative invention that teaches and moves. Different standards apply per kind.

rubrics_metrics.name: True poets should make things better than nature or quite anew
rubrics_metrics.description: True poets “make things either better than nature bringeth forth, or quite anew; forms such as never were in nature, as the heroes, demi-gods, Cyclops, chimeras, furies, and such like.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creativity and invention are essential: the poet’s power is to idealize or create novel forms. Judge the success of invention by its internal plausibility, moral/educative power, and capacity to delight the mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substance over form — versifying is not the essence of poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is not rhyming and versing that maketh a poet ... but it is that feigning notable images of virtues, vices, or what else, with that delightful teaching, which must be the right describing note to know a poet by.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate metrical ornament with poetic quality. A good poem may be prose (Xenophon, Heliodorus); conversely, mere versifiers may lack true poetic invention. Assess based on imaginative content and didactic-delightful effect, not only on verse form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre and manner must fit subject — measured, proportioned language
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets choose verse as “their fittest raiment ... piecing each syllable of each word by just proportion, according to the dignity of the subject.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Style (meter, diction, tone) should be proportionate to subject-matter. Evaluate whether language, rhythm, and stylistic choices suit the subject’s dignity and purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry’s moral efficacy — teaching virtue by delighting
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets “imitate to teach and delight, and delight to move men to take that goodness in hand, which, without delight they would fly as from a stranger; and teach to make them know that goodness whereunto they are moved.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A key test is whether the poem not only describes virtue but makes virtuous action desirable and imaginable. Measure a poem’s ethical power by its ability to motivate readers through pleasurable presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry as educator: purifying wit, enriching memory, enabling judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry purifies wit, enriches memory, enables judgment, and enlarges conceit — leading and drawing us toward higher perfection and virtuous action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the poem’s educative impact: does it sharpen intellect, lodge memorable images, refine judgment, and expand imaginative capacity toward moral ends?

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventiveness disciplined by learned discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: True poets should “range only, reined with learned discretion, into the divine consideration of what may be, and should be.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creative freedom must be exercised with judgment and knowledge. Evaluate whether imaginative departures are guided by discernment (taste, learning) rather than mere fanciful excess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of vivid particularities and passionate description
rubrics_metrics.description: Sidney notes poets’ contribution of “passionate describing of passions, the many particularities of battles ... or long orations, put in the months of great kings and captains.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge descriptive power: the specificity and emotional vividness should illuminate characters and situations, making lessons memorable and affecting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagery — poetry as a 'speaking picture'
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry is described metaphorically as “a speaking picture.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the strength and aptness of images: do they paint scenes or ideas that speak to the mind’s eye and serve the poem’s instructive and delightful purposes?

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre taxonomy — choice among heroic, lyric, tragic, comic, pastoral, etc.
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets are subdivided into heroic, lyric, tragic, comic, satyric, iambic, elegiac, pastoral, and certain others; some are termed by matter, some by verse form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the poem’s genre and apply genre-appropriate expectations (e.g., tragic pathos, pastoral simplicity, heroic grandeur). A work should satisfy the norms and aims of its declared or evident genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meter and musicality where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference to Psalms being “fully written in metre” and the ancient regard for “number and measure in the words” as giving poetic force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When rhythm and musicality are integral to the kind of poem, judge the effectiveness of meter, cadence, and musical devices in enhancing both delight and distinctness of expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet as mediator between historian and moral philosopher
rubrics_metrics.description: Sidney argues the poet can surpass historians and moral philosophers by providing example and precept: historians give experience; philosophers give precept; the poet gives both in an attractive form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how well a poem synthesizes exemplary narrative (historical/illustrative) and ethical insight: the best poetry furnishes living examples that teach as effectively as precept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry’s priority in cultural initiation and popular education
rubrics_metrics.description: Sidney argues poets were the first light-givers to ignorance and the nursery of learning in many nations (e.g., Homer, Hesiod; Dante, Petrarch; Chaucer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider a poem’s capacity to introduce and popularize knowledge or virtues for wider audiences; accessibility and formative power are virtues in this light.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of idle or corrupt uses — not mere amusement or vice
rubrics_metrics.description: Sidney rebukes those who ‘bark at’ poetry from ignorance and warns against poetry that leads to idle appetite or corrupts; poetry should not be a feeder of idle appetite divorced from virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the poem’s delights promote virtuous ends rather than merely catering to base appetites or immoral examples; beware of works that delight but do not instruct or that instruct toward vice.
